title: Determinants of lung cancer screening follow-up care in community care settings: A qualitative multi-case study in the ACCELL trial.
authors: Palazzo L, Hansell L, Wernli KJ et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adherence to lung cancer screening (LCS) follow-up is essential to achieve mortality benefits from screening. However, population-based studies demonstrate follow-up is <50% in clinical settings. Determinants (barriers and facilitators) of LCS follow-up in community settings are under-studied.
RESEARCH QUESTION: What are determinants of LCS follow-up in community settings?
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: This qualitative multi-case study informed a pre-post intervention trial, testing pragmatic interventions to address LCS follow-up in community settings. We conducted rapid ethnographic assessments (REA) through virtual and in person site visits of LCS delivery in three community-based healthcare systems in Washington state. Additionally at the two future intervention sites, we conducted provider and patient interviews. Interview transcripts were analyzed using Rapid Group Analysis Process. All data were triangulated according to Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities Research Framework domains.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight organizational leaders, providers, and staff participated in REA. Thirty-one patients and 15 providers from the future intervention sites participated in interviews. Determinants of LCS follow-up in the intervention domain included role of primary care, LCS complexity and care process standardization. In the inner setting domain (organization and clinic), screening prioritization, EHR use, radiology support, and context of wellness visits affected LCS. The main theme in the outer setting domain was the influence of social determinants of health on LCS. In the individuals domain, shared beliefs in LCS and LCS education and information sharing were key. In the process implementation domain, clinical champions and use of data and metrics were crucial.
INTERPRETATION: Integrated findings suggest determinants related to LCS complexity, care fragmentation, socioeconomic status and language, and limitations of PCPs could be overcome through more centralized approaches. However, increased use of EHR tools, increased education and standardizing LCS performance metrics may enable follow-up in decentralized settings.
CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: NCT06324110.

title: Escalation of Resting Heart Rate and Tachycardia as a Response to Thoracic Radiotherapy: Implications for Cardiovascular Outcomes after Radiotherapy.
authors: Ajdari A, Bobic M, Ciausu C et al.
journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiac toxicity is a well-recognized, but poorly understood complication of radiotherapy (RT). In non-oncological settings, there is an established relationship between resting heart rate and cardiovascular health.
OBJECTIVES: To study the incidence and pattern of resting heart rate (rHR) as an early sign of cardiotoxicity among patients with non-metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with RT.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed serial rHR measurements of consecutive patients with locally advanced NSCLC treated with definitive chemoradiation (CRT) over 6-7 weeks of daily radiation treatments followed by immunotherapy (durvalumab) between 2017-2022. Radiation dose to the heart and 17 cardiac substructures were extracted. Associations between heart rate elevation, tachycardia, cardiac substructure dose and outcomes were evaluated using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and regression analysis.
RESULTS: We identified 110 patients, 56.4% with pre-existing heart disease. Median follow-up was 33.6 months. Median age was 70.4 years. Median rHR increased significantly during RT, rising from 81.5 bpm to 93 bpm at end of RT (p < 0.0001), remaining elevated in 30.6% of patients 12 months post-RT. Tachycardia incidence rose from 11.2% at baseline to 36.5% at 1-month post-RT (p < 0.0001). After adjusting for comorbidities, higher mean sinoatrial node (SAN) dose was associated with higher rHR elevation, delayed HR recovery and persistent tachycardia (all p < 0.05). Higher rHR during and after RT (β = 0.23, p = 0.005, and β = 13.49, p = 0.049, respectively), as well as the incidence of tachycardia episodes during RT were associated with increased odds of developing an arrhythmia (OR, 2.97, 95% CI, 1.17-7.52, p = 0.022).
CONCLUSIONS: Elevated rHR and tachycardia are observed during and after RT for NSCLC and are associated with higher mean SAN dose. HR elevation was associated with increased risk of de novo arrhythmias, suggesting that heart rate may represent a non-invasive biomarker of subclinical cardiac injury. Prospective studies might be warranted to test the potential of routine HR monitoring and proactive dose reductions to the SAN to enable early detection and help mitigate the risk of post-treatment arrhythmia.

title: Differential Diagnosis of Lung Cancer Using Artificial Intelligence-Based Extracellular Vesicle Analysis: A Pilot Study.
authors: Yoon HB, Choi BH, Kim S et al.
abstract: In cancer diagnosis, liquid biopsy is a minimally invasive method, yet its diagnostic performance is constrained by insufficient sensitivity and restricted blood biomarkers. Therefore, the use of additional invasive methods is unavoidable to identify cancer-specific information, such as subtypes, stages, and mutation status. Here, we propose a deep-learning-based method for differential diagnosis, in which group-specific feature importance is assigned to Raman spectra of extracellular vesicles (EVs) and the spectra are decoded. The feature importance was extracted from the training dataset using explainable AI (XAI) to emphasize key spectral patterns. These features were then applied to the original spectra as weights to develop an AI-based diagnostic algorithm. As a result, the algorithm successfully identified the presence of lung cancer, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.98. Moreover, it demonstrated the capability of precision cancer diagnosis with an average AUC of 0.96 across the detailed cancer information. These preliminary findings suggest the potential of liquid-biopsy-based differential diagnosis and its possible contribution to the establishment of rapid and tailored treatment strategies.

title: EQD2-adjusted mean lung dose and symptomatic pneumonitis after thoracic radiotherapy following immune checkpoint inhibitors in lung cancer: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
authors: Li X, Liu L, Zheng N et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evidence on pneumonitis after thoracic radiotherapy following immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) exposure remains limited. We examined associations with voxel-wise EQD2 mean lung dose (MLDEQD2) and the ICI-radiotherapy interval.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 98 patients in a 90-day competing-risk analysis of grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis (CTCAE), comprising 26 pneumonitis events, 70 event-free observations, and two deaths before pneumonitis. Archived DICOM doses were converted voxel-wise using α/β = 3 Gy. Cumulative incidence was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method, and Fine-Gray regression included continuous MLDEQD2 and treatment interval. Supplementary logistic analyses included 96 patients.
RESULTS: The 90-day pneumonitis cumulative incidence was 26.5% (95% CI 17.7%-35.3%). The adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio (SHR) for MLDEQD2 was 1.339 per Gy (95% CI 1.113-1.612; P = 0.002). The interval SHR was 0.784 per 10 days (95% CI 0.639-0.963; P = 0.020). Physical MLD showed a consistent association (SHR 1.197 per Gy, 95% CI 1.036-1.382; P = 0.015).
CONCLUSION: Higher MLDEQD2 and shorter treatment intervals were associated with grade ≥2 symptomatic pneumonitis in this treatment sequence. Clinical ascertainment and dose-reconstruction uncertainties limit interpretation. The absence of an ICI-naive comparator precludes conclusions about ICI-specific radiosensitization. Prospective validation is required before these associations can inform dose constraints or treatment scheduling.

title: Durvalumab completion and re-administration after grade 2 radiation pneumonitis following concurrent chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III NSCLC: a single-center real-world study.
authors: Aoki S, Ariyasu R, Kamima T et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: This study evaluated the incidence and clinical impact of radiation pneumonitis (RP) in patients with unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with durvalumab following concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT), with a particular focus on durvalumab interruption, re-administration, and overall survival (OS).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included patients treated at our institution between April 2018 and June 2024. Durvalumab was administered for up to one year or until discontinuation due to adverse events or disease progression. RP was graded according to CTCAE version 5.0. Associations between grade ≥ 2 RP and clinical or treatment-related factors were assessed using univariate and multivariate analyses. Survival outcomes were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS: Among 101 patients, 48 (47.5%) developed grade ≥ 2 RP (grade 2: 41.6%; grade 3: 4.0%; grade 4: 2.0%). Lung V20 > 30% was independently associated with grade ≥ 2 RP. Durvalumab interruption occurred in a subset of patients with grade 2 RP; among these patients, 25 (59.5%) were able to undergo durvalumab re-administration, with RP recurrence observed in only one patient after re-administration. The 2-year and 3-year OS rates were 75.1% and 60.9%, respectively. Completion of durvalumab was the strongest independent predictor of OS (hazard ratio 0.14; P = 0.00007), whereas grade ≥ 2 RP itself was not significantly associated with OS.
CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world cohort, completion of durvalumab consolidation after CCRT was strongly associated with improved OS in patients with stage III NSCLC. Although grade ≥ 2 RP was a frequent complication, temporary interruption and re-administration were feasible in selected patients. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the retrospective design and potential residual confounding.

title: Acceptability of a web-based decision aid for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer treatment selection: A prospective pilot study.
authors: Kobayashi N, Takeda A, Muraoka S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: For clinical stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), treatment selection between surgery and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) can be preference sensitive. Accordingly, we developed a web-based patient decision aid (PDA) and prospectively evaluated its patient-reported utility in routine respiratory clinical practice.
METHODS: This prospective pilot study enrolled 26 patients with clinical stage I NSCLC or suspected primary lung cancer (cT1-2aN0M0) considered candidates for surgery and SBRT at two Japanese hospitals between October 2023 and December 2024. Patients used the PDA before finalizing treatment through shared decision-making. Outcomes were patient-perceived utility, Decisional Conflict Scale (DCS) scores measured once after the decision, and treatment preference transitions.
RESULTS: Twenty-four patients completed the PDA evaluation. All participants reported improved knowledge or understanding, 18 (75.0%) reported reduced anxiety, and 23 (95.8%) reported that the PDA was useful. Final treatment selection was SBRT in 15 (57.7%), surgery in nine (34.6%), and observation in two (7.7%), with no significant difference by histological confirmation at enrollment (p = 0.59). In the exploratory post-decision DCS analysis of 22 patients, those who underwent surgery had numerically higher uncertainty scores than those who underwent SBRT (29.2 vs. 14.9). The PDA mainly clarified preferences among initially undecided patients.
CONCLUSIONS: The web-based PDA was acceptable, and participants reported improved understanding and reduced anxiety. Because the DCS was administered only after treatment selection, its effect on decisional conflict could not be evaluated. Controlled evaluation of PDA-supported shared decision-making for early-stage NSCLC is warranted.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry, UMIN000052599.

title: A Phase 1 Trial Investigating the Addition of Papaverine to Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT) for Hypoxic Radiosensitization of Lung Tumors.
authors: Brownstein J, Williams T, Xu-Welliver M et al.
journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tumor hypoxia has been recognized as a barrier to effective radiotherapy. Preclinical work identified the FDA approved smooth muscle relaxant papaverine (PPV) as having an "off target" activity as a mitochondrial inhibitor that reduces hypoxia and radiosensitizes model tumors.
METHODS: We conducted an IRB-approved phase 1 clinical trial to evaluate safety and feasibility of adding PPV to stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for tumors of the lung. Eligible patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or limited lung metastases who were candidates for SBRT (50 Gy in 4 or 5 fractions) were enrolled. Based on a Bayesian Optimal Interval (BOIN) design, patients were allocated to receive PPV 30-90 minutes prior to each SBRT fraction at 3 dose levels (DL): 0.5 mg/kg (DL-1), 1 mg/kg (DL1), or 2mg/kg (DL2).
RESULTS: Nineteen patients enrolled and 18 completed study treatment and were evaluable, with a median follow up of 33.4 months. Among 18 evaluable patients, 7 had early-stage NSCLC, 2 had metastatic NSCLC, and 8 had lung metastases from other histologies. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was determined to be DL2, which had a dose limiting toxicity (DLT) rate posterior estimate of 0.17 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.53). The 2-year controls rates for local, regional and distant control were 100%, 94% and 82%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate the feasibility and safety of PPV as a hypoxic radiosensitizer for SBRT. The MTD for this patient population is at least 2 mg/kg of PPV. Encouraging clinical results indicate that further investigation of PPV's utility as a tumor-selective radiosensitizer is warranted.

title: HMGB1 directly activates BAP1 transcription to sustain tumor growth in mesothelioma.
authors: Novelli F, Giannakou L, Wang Z et al.
abstract: BAP1 and HMGB1 alterations are implicated in the pathogenesis of mesothelioma, an aggressive cancer of the membranes covering the thoracic and abdominal cavities. Genetic inactivating mutations of BAP1 cause cancer in ~100% of carriers. The mechanism/s that regulate BAP1 expression were unknown. We discovered that HMGB1 directly modulates BAP1 expression. Studying our Hmgb1 knock-out mouse mesothelioma models, primary fibroblasts obtained from carriers of pathogenic heterozygous germline BAP1 mutations, and mesothelioma cell lines, we discovered that HMGB1 loss caused a significant reduction in BAP1 expression and protein levels, whereas HMGB1 overexpression increased BAP1 mRNA and protein levels. We demonstrated that HMGB1 binds to the BAP1 promoter and activates its transcription, leading to BAP1 overexpression, which in turn promoted the proliferation, migration, and invasion of mesothelioma cells. These findings were confirmed in lung, colon, and cholangiocarcinoma cell lines. These findings indicate that while BAP1 inactivating mutations promote cancer development, cancer cells that do not express BAP1 are less aggressive, pointing to the HMGB1-BAP1 axis as a novel attractive target for therapy. Furthermore, our discovery that HMGB1-driven BAP1 overexpression supports cancer growth provides a mechanistic rationale for the improved survival observed in mesothelioma patients with somatic BAP1 inactivating mutations.

title: Monoamine Oxidase A Expression Marks Aged Progenitor Signatures in Thymic Epithelial Cells and Thymomas.
authors: Matsumoto M, Hanibuchi Y, Otsuka K et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The biological basis distinguishing thymomas from thymic carcinomas (TCs) remains incompletely defined, despite longstanding efforts to interpret thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) in relation to thymic epithelial cell (TEC) differentiation. We integrated single-cell transcriptomic, immunohistochemical, and bulk transcriptomic analyses to define TEC programs associated with TET subtypes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We reanalyzed a publicly available human thymus single-cell RNA-seq dataset to define signature genes of TEC subclusters. Immunohistochemistry was performed on non-neoplastic thymus across developmental stages and on 83 TETs. Transcriptomic analyses were conducted using the TCGA-THYM cohort comprising 117 TETs.
RESULTS: We identified an adult-enriched TEC subset with an aged progenitor-like program, marked by monoamine oxidase A (MAOA). Strikingly, MAOA immunohistochemistry highlighted spindle-shaped epithelial cells in the involuted adult thymus and in type A/AB thymomas. Most type B3 thymomas also exhibited broad MAOA reactivity, whereas TCs were negative or showed only scattered tumor-cell staining. Furthermore, MAOA immunostaining complemented KIT in the distinction between thymomas and TCs. In the TCGA-THYM cohort, MAOA expression reproduced these subtype-associated patterns and correlated with aged progenitor signatures. TEC signature scoring further revealed enrichment of aged progenitor-like programs in type A/AB thymomas, while type B3 thymomas concomitantly exhibited aged progenitor-like and cortical TEC-like signatures. In marked contrast, TCs showed low levels of aged progenitor scores but prominent mature medullary TEC signatures.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings refine the biological framework of TETs by linking thymomas to an aged progenitor-like TEC state. MAOA also offers practical diagnostic utility, particularly for distinguishing thymomas from TCs.

title: Assessment of Q-PCR based vector copy numbers and viral titration in CAR T cell products, Probe vs SYBR Green.
summary: Assessment of vector copy numbers (VCNs) in comprised of the chimeric antigen receptor (CAR (T cells as a safety parameter and viral titration in the vector bank (VB) as an efficacy parameter are essential in the CAR T cell production procedure. Here, we developed a quantitative-PCR (Q-PCR) based VCN and viral titration analysis using both Probe and SYBR Green methods. Cellular viral titration was also applied for comparison of viral titration results. The VCN in CAR T cells with SYBR Green was 1.72, 2.31, and 2.46 respectively, while in the Probe based analysis, it was 1.33, 1.83, and 2.20. The molecular viral titration in SYBR Green resulted in 2.90*109, 5.24*1010, and 9.76*1010, while in the Probe it was 1.54*109, 1.13*109, and 7.73*108. The cellular titration resulted in 1.73*106, 2.16*106, and 2.49*106. In summary, both SYBR Green and Probe revealing that Probe strategy had a lower dependency on sample contamination and could be a better strategy for the Q-PCR method. The SYBR Green based viral titration method is significantly different from the Probe based method, with the Probe based method yielding better results compared to the cellular titration method. However, no significant difference was reported in both methods for VCNs.

title: Engineered T cells controlled by granulocyte colony-stimulating factor eradicate murine melanoma without lymphodepletion or interleukin-2
summary: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy can be effective against metastatic melanoma, including immune checkpoint-resistant disease, but current protocols require lymphodepletion and high-dose interleukin-2 (IL-2), which can cause substantial toxicity. To overcome this limitation, we engineered a chimeric receptor, G2R, that generates an IL-2-like proliferative signal in response to granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), a well-tolerated cytokine widely used in oncology. Human T cells expressing G2R expanded in vitro in response to G-CSF in place of IL-2 or interleukin-15 (IL-15), and the three cytokines induced broadly similar intracellular signalling and cytokine secretion profiles. In immune-competent mice bearing established B16-F10 melanoma, adoptive transfer of G2R-expressing, tumour-reactive CD8+ T cells followed by systemic G-CSF treatment induced profound T cell expansion. This was accompanied by complete, durable tumour regression in over 75% of animals without the need for lymphodepletion, exogenous IL-2 or any other therapy. G-CSF treatment induced transient neutrophil expansion in peripheral blood but no increase in intratumoural neutrophils or macrophages. G2R-expressing memory T cells persisted long-term and could be re-expanded upon G-CSF re-treatment, enabling rejection of second tumour challenges. Thus, G-CSF can be repurposed to enable clinician-controlled anti-tumour T cell responses of profound magnitude, efficacy and durability, an approach that is readily translatable to humans.
